Inequality is a noun that describes the condition of not being equal — when two or more things, people, or groups differ in a way that matters: in size, amount, value, rights, power, or opportunity. It names a gap, an imbalance, an unevenness between things being compared.

Think of a set of scales. When both sides weigh the same, you have equality — perfect balance. When one side is heavier and the other is lighter, that imbalance is inequality. The opposite of inequality is always equality.

"Inequality" is used meaningfully in three distinct worlds: everyday conversation, social and economic discussion, and mathematics. Knowing all three makes you fully fluent with the word.

In Everyday Language

In its most basic sense, inequality refers to any noticeable imbalance or difference between things — and it doesn't have to involve people or fairness at all.

"There is a clear inequality in the quality of the two roads."
"The inequality in the sizes of the two rooms is obvious."

Here it simply means: one thing is measurably less than, worse than, or smaller than something it is being compared to.

In Social and Economic Contexts — The Most Common Use

This is where you will most often encounter this word, and it's where it carries the most weight.

Social inequality refers to the uneven distribution of rights, power, status, and opportunity among people or groups in a society. Economic inequality refers to the uneven distribution of money and wealth — some individuals or groups possessing vastly more than others.

Imagine 100 people standing in a field. If 10 of them own 90% of everything, while the other 90 share just 10%, that gap is economic inequality in plain view.

Some of the most discussed types include income inequality (people earning vastly different amounts for their work), gender inequality (women and men not being treated the same in law, in the workplace, or in society), racial inequality (people of different races facing different opportunities and treatment), educational inequality (some children accessing far better schools and resources than others), and health inequality (certain groups facing worse access to healthcare or worse health outcomes).

In this context, inequality isn't just a neutral description. It carries real moral weight. It implies that something is unfair — that people are not receiving the same dignity, the same chances, or the same treatment that they deserve. That's why you'll consistently find it paired with calls for action: addressing inequality, reducing inequality, fighting inequality.

One important nuance: social inequality doesn't mean that everyone must be identical or end up with identical outcomes in life. It means that everyone deserves the same fundamental rights, dignity, and basic opportunities — and wherever that isn't happening, inequality exists.

In Mathematics

In mathematics, an inequality is a precise statement that two quantities or expressions are not equal, and specifically that one is greater than or less than the other. This is expressed using symbols: < means "less than," > means "greater than," ≤ means "less than or equal to," and ≥ means "greater than or equal to."

So the statement 3 < 7 is a mathematical inequality. It tells you not just that the numbers differ, but how they differ — 3 is the smaller of the two.

In algebra, inequalities describe ranges of possible values rather than a single fixed answer. The inequality x > 5 means x could be 6, 10, 100, or any number greater than 5. There are infinitely many valid answers, which is unlike an equation that pins you to exactly one answer.

Inequality in the singular describes the broad condition or state of being unequal, usually spoken of in the abstract: "Inequality is one of the defining challenges of our era."

Inequalities in the plural refers to specific, individual instances or types of unevenness: "The report revealed deep inequalities in how different neighborhoods were funded."

Both are common, and choosing between them depends on whether you're talking about the concept as a whole or about particular examples of it.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Inequality vs. difference. Every inequality involves a difference, but not every difference is an inequality. The fact that your shirt is red and mine is blue is a difference — not an inequality. Inequality implies a difference that matters: in value, power, fairness, or quantity. A difference becomes an inequality when it puts one side at a disadvantage or creates an imbalance that is measurable or meaningful.

Inequality vs. inequity. These two words are close cousins and are often used interchangeably, but they have a meaningful nuance. Inequality describes the measurable gap itself — it is relatively neutral. Inequity adds a moral judgment: the gap is not merely a gap; it is unfair and unjust. All inequities involve inequality, but not every inequality is an inequity (some differences are natural, acceptable, or even appropriate). In everyday conversation, however, many people treat them as the same word, and in most contexts you won't be wrong to use them interchangeably.

Inequality vs. disparity. Disparity is a near-synonym meaning a great and often troubling difference. The subtle distinction: disparity tends to emphasize the sheer size of the gap, while inequality more often emphasizes the imbalance in fairness or standing. In practice, the two words are largely interchangeable and you will often see them used side by side.

Knowing which words naturally accompany "inequality" will sharpen your feel for it enormously.

Rising or growing inequality means the gap is getting wider over time. Stark inequality describes a gap that is especially dramatic and obvious. Systemic inequality describes inequality that is deeply embedded in the laws, institutions, and structures of a society — it is not caused by individual bad behavior alone, but is baked into the system itself. To address, reduce, or tackle inequality means to take action to make things more equal. To widen inequality means a policy, event, or force is making the gap larger, not smaller.

Everyday: "There is a noticeable inequality in the resources given to rural versus urban schools."

Social: "Decades of neglect have deepened the inequality between the wealthy and the working poor."

Economic: "The gap in income inequality between the top 1% and everyone else has widened significantly."

Mathematical: "Solve the inequality: 2x + 3 > 7." / "Unlike an equation, an inequality can have an infinite number of valid solutions."

Whether in conversation, in society, or in mathematics, inequality always points to the same central truth: a gap in which one side ends up with less — less money, less power, less opportunity, or simply a lower value. In human contexts especially, it names not just a measurement but a problem — one that implies the gap deserves to be questioned, challenged, or closed. In mathematics, it is a clean and precise tool for describing how values relate to each other.

Mastering this word means holding both its descriptive power (it objectively names and measures a gap) and its moral charge (in human contexts, it implies that gap is worth confronting).
